name: Grammarly
tagline: AI writing assistant with grammar, tone detection, and style suggestions
verdictSummary: A grammar checker that calls an LLM API with a proofreading prompt works well for basic spelling and grammar. You can one-shot a text editor with a 'check grammar' button. But Grammarly's real product is tone detection (confidence, formality, politeness scores), real-time inline suggestions across every text field (browser extension at OS level), and the clarity/engagement rewrites that require sophisticated language models.
coreLoopDIY: Text editor with AI-powered grammar and style checking via LLM API
whatYouLose: Tone detection with scores (confident, formal, friendly, etc.)
Full-sentence rewrites for clarity and engagement
Style guide and brand tone customization
whyPeopleStillPay: Real-time corrections in every text field (email, docs, social media) via the browser extension, plus tone guidance that generic AI can't match

priorArt.name: LanguageTool Open-source grammar and style checker and the primary Grammarly-like prior art. ↗
priorArt.desc: LanguageTool Open-source grammar and style checker and the primary Grammarly-like prior art. ↗

notes: LanguageTool is a solid open-source alternative. The tone detection is Grammarly's unique selling point.
prompt:
Build me a personal writing checker to replace Grammarly. Requirements:

- Grammar engine: LanguageTool running locally via its official Docker image;
  grammar checks never leave my machine.
- A local web page (Node + Express, binds to localhost): paste text, see
  LanguageTool issues underlined with hover explanations, click a suggestion
  to apply it.
- An LLM rewrite pane (key in .env) with three buttons: tighten, friendlier,
  formal. Show a diff against my original before I accept anything.
- A personal dictionary file (dictionary.txt) of names and jargon to never
  flag, passed to LanguageTool on every check.
- CLI mode: `check <file.md>` prints issues with line numbers, exits nonzero
  if any, so it can run as a git pre-commit hook on docs.
- Everything local except the optional LLM call; no accounts, no telemetry.
- Out of scope: a browser extension and inline suggestions inside Gmail,
  Docs, or Slack. This is a destination I paste into, that is the honest
  trade against Grammarly.
- README: Docker setup for LanguageTool, the roughly 1 GB of RAM it wants,
  and where the LLM key goes.
